config.title: Micro-frontend Shell

intro.title: Micro-frontend Shell
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple micro-frontend shell application that acts as a container for loading and displaying other micro-frontends. You will learn the core concept of dynamic component loading using React's lazy and Suspense features. The main technologies involved are React with TypeScript for type safety and React Router for basic navigation. This project will help you understand how to structure a host application that can integrate separate, independently developed frontend modules.
intro.usecase: Micro-frontend shell architecture is commonly used in enterprise applications where multiple teams develop independent features that must integrate into a unified interface. Examples include large e-commerce platforms where different teams handle product listings, shopping cart, and checkout modules, all loading within a single shell application. Financial dashboards at banks often use this pattern to combine trading interfaces, portfolio management, and analytics tools from separate codebases. Content management systems like WordPress or Drupal employ micro-frontend shells to allow plugin developers to build isolated UI components that integrate seamlessly. This approach enables scalable development while maintaining consistent navigation and user experience across complex applications.

objectives: Apply TypeScript interfaces to define the structure of micro-frontend configuration objects
Implement a React component to serve as the main shell container for micro-frontends
Use React Router to define navigation routes within the shell application
Construct dynamic import statements to load micro-frontend modules on demand
Execute conditional rendering logic to display micro-frontends based on current route
Define state management hooks to track the loading status of micro-frontend modules
Handle asynchronous operations to fetch and initialize micro-frontend components
Utilize error boundaries to gracefully handle failures in micro-frontend loading
Assign CSS classes and styling to create consistent layout containers for embedded content
Control component lifecycle to properly mount and unmount micro-frontends during navigation
Access configuration data to determine which micro-frontends to load for specific routes
Modify component props to pass shared context and data to loaded micro-frontends

steps.title: Import React and useState from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from 'react'.
steps.expectedOutcome: The React library and useState hook are imported, making them available for use in the component.
successCriteria: The import statement correctly imports React and useState from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState, which are essential for building React components with state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackWrong: That's not quite right. You need to import React and useState from the 'react' package using an import statement.

steps.title: Create the MicroFrontendShell component
steps.instruction: Define a functional component named MicroFrontendShell that returns null for now.
steps.hint: Create a component using either a function declaration or arrow function. Make sure it returns null.
steps.expectedOutcome: A functional component named MicroFrontendShell is created and returns null.
successCriteria: The component is defined with the correct name and returns null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the MicroFrontendShell component. This is the shell that will host your micro-frontends.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure the component is named exactly 'MicroFrontendShell' and returns null.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component wasn't created correctly. Check that you've defined a component named 'MicroFrontendShell' that returns null.

steps.title: Define the component props interface
steps.instruction: Create an interface named MicroFrontendShellProps with a single property called microFrontends of type string[].
steps.hint: Use the TypeScript interface keyword to define the props interface. The property should be typed as an array of strings.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a TypeScript interface that defines the expected props for your MicroFrontendShell component.
successCriteria: The interface must be named MicroFrontendShellProps and must include a microFrontends property of type string[].
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the props interface with the correct type.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that your interface has the exact name and property type specified.
steps.feedbackWrong: The interface definition doesn't match the requirements. Make sure you're using the TypeScript interface syntax with the correct property type.

steps.title: Add props to the component
steps.instruction: Add the MicroFrontendShellProps interface as the type for the component's props parameter.
steps.hint: In TypeScript, you can type the component's props by adding them as a parameter with the interface name after a colon.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component function now accepts typed props using the MicroFrontendShellProps interface.
successCriteria: The component function has a props parameter
The props parameter is typed with MicroFrontendShellProps
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the props interface to your component. This ensures TypeScript will validate the props passed to your component.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the props parameter is explicitly typed with the MicroFrontendShellProps interface.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component doesn't have the props parameter typed with the MicroFrontendShellProps interface. Try adding the props parameter with the correct type annotation.

steps.title: Initialize active micro-frontend state
steps.instruction: Inside your MicroFrontendShell component, initialize a state variable named 'activeMicroFrontend' using useState. Set its initial value to the first item in props.microFrontends if the array exists and has items, otherwise default to an empty string.
steps.hint: Use useState with a generic type of string. You can access props.microFrontends[0] for the default value, but handle the case when the array might be empty.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now has a state variable 'activeMicroFrontend' that tracks which micro-frontend is currently active, with a sensible default value.
successCriteria: State variable named 'activeMicroFrontend' is declared
Uses useState hook with string type
Initial value is props.microFrontends[0] or empty string
Properly handles empty array case
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the active micro-frontend state. The useState hook will help track which micro-frontend should be displayed.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check: Did you name the state variable 'activeMicroFrontend'? Did you handle the case when props.microFrontends might be empty?
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's focus on this step: Inside the component, use useState to create a state variable named 'activeMicroFrontend' with type string. The initial value should be the first item from props.microFrontends if available, otherwise an empty string.

steps.title: Create handler to change active micro-frontend
steps.instruction: Inside your MicroFrontendShell component, create a function named handleMicroFrontendChange that takes a microFrontend parameter of type string and sets the activeMicroFrontend state to that value.
steps.hint: Define the function using either a function declaration or arrow function syntax. The function should call the setActiveMicroFrontend function with the parameter value.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a handleMicroFrontendChange function that takes a string parameter and calls setActiveMicroFrontend with that parameter.
successCriteria: The function must be named handleMicroFrontendChange, accept a string parameter, and call setActiveMicroFrontend with that parameter.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the handler function that will update the active micro-frontend state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that your function: 1) is named handleMicroFrontendChange, 2) accepts a string parameter, and 3) calls setActiveMicroFrontend with that parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handler function isn't quite right. Make sure you create a function named handleMicroFrontendChange that takes a string parameter and calls setActiveMicroFrontend with it.

steps.title: Return a container div
steps.instruction: In the component's return statement, replace the existing div with a div element that has a className of 'micro-frontend-shell'.
steps.hint: Update the JSX to return a div with the specified className attribute.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component returns a div with className='micro-frontend-shell' as its root element.
successCriteria: The component's return statement should contain a div element with the className attribute set to 'micro-frontend-shell'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the container div with the correct className. This provides the basic structure for your micro-frontend shell.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're returning a div element with exactly className='micro-frontend-shell'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component doesn't return a div with className='micro-frontend-shell'. Check that you've updated the return statement correctly.

steps.title: Add navigation section
steps.instruction: Inside the container div, add a <nav> element with the className 'micro-frontend-nav'.
steps.hint: Use the <nav> HTML element to create a navigation section. Add the className attribute with the value 'micro-frontend-nav'.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component's return statement now includes a <nav> element with the correct className inside the container div.
successCriteria: The code should contain a <nav> element with className='micro-frontend-nav' placed inside the existing container <div>.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the navigation section. This will serve as the area where users can select different micro-frontends.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but there might be a small issue. Make sure you've added a <nav> element with exactly className='micro-frontend-nav' inside the container div.
steps.feedbackWrong: The navigation section wasn't added correctly. You need to add a <nav> element with className='micro-frontend-nav' inside the existing container div.

steps.title: Create navigation buttons for each micro-frontend
steps.instruction: Inside the navigation section, use the map method on props.microFrontends to create a button element for each micro-frontend name. Each button should display the micro-frontend name as its text content.
steps.hint: You can use props.microFrontends.map() to iterate. Inside the map callback, return a <button> element with the micro-frontend name as its children.
steps.expectedOutcome: The navigation section will contain a button for each micro-frontend name passed in the microFrontends prop.
successCriteria: Use props.microFrontends.map()
Return a <button> element for each item
Display the micro-frontend name as button text
Include a key prop on each button
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created dynamic navigation buttons for each micro-frontend. This allows users to see all available micro-frontends at a glance.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check if you're: 1) using props.microFrontends.map(), 2) returning a button element for each item, 3) displaying the micro-frontend name as button text, and 4) including a key prop.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. You need to map over the microFrontends array from props and create a button for each item. Remember to use the map method and return JSX for each button.

steps.title: Wire button clicks to handler
steps.instruction: Add an onClick handler to each button that calls handleMicroFrontendChange with the corresponding micro-frontend name.
steps.hint: Use the onClick attribute on the button element and call the handler with the current microFrontend value from the map.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of wiring a button click to a handler
<button onClick={() => handleClick(item)}>{item}</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: Each button will now trigger the handleMicroFrontendChange function when clicked, passing the appropriate micro-frontend name.
successCriteria: The button elements inside the map function should have an onClick handler that calls handleMicroFrontendChange with the current microFrontend value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully wired the button clicks to the handler. Each button now calls handleMicroFrontendChange with the correct micro-frontend name when clicked.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the onClick handler might be missing or not correctly calling handleMicroFrontendChange with the microFrontend value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The buttons don't have the correct onClick handlers. Make sure each button calls handleMicroFrontendChange with the current microFrontend value from the map.

steps.title: Add content area for active micro-frontend
steps.instruction: Add a <main> element with className 'micro-frontend-content' after the closing </nav> tag to display the active micro-frontend.
steps.hint: Place the <main> element as a sibling to the <nav> element, inside the container <div>. Use the activeMicroFrontend state variable to display the selected micro-frontend name.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a content area that displays the currently selected micro-frontend name.
successCriteria: Add a <main> element after the <nav> element
Set className to 'micro-frontend-content'
Display the activeMicroFrontend state variable inside the <main> element
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the content area that will display the active micro-frontend. The <main> element with the 'micro-frontend-content' class is now ready to show which micro-frontend is selected.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that you've added the <main> element after the <nav> element, given it the className 'micro-frontend-content', and included the activeMicroFrontend variable inside it.
steps.feedbackWrong: The content area for the active micro-frontend hasn't been added correctly. Make sure to add a <main> element with className 'micro-frontend-content' after the navigation, and display the activeMicroFrontend state variable inside it.

steps.title: Display the active micro-frontend in content area
steps.instruction: Inside the content area (after the navigation), add a paragraph element that displays the currently selected micro-frontend. Use the activeMicroFrontend state variable to show its value.

successCriteria:

steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a paragraph that displays the active micro-frontend. The UI now shows which micro-frontend is currently selected.
